newsitem.title: IRAQ: Iraq obstructs U.N. flights, says arms inspector.
newsitem.headline: Iraq obstructs U.N. flights, says arms inspector.

text.p: The U.N.'s chief arms inspector for Iraq complained on Saturday that Baghdad was obstructing flights by U.N. helicopters, sometimes going so far as to risk the lives of pilots and experts on board.

In his first complaint about the operation of the U.N.'s monitoring system in Iraq, Rolf Ekeus said his experts had recently noted a "serious deterioration in Iraqi performance. We have seen a tendency to block, undercut, make our helicopter operations dangerous and difficult."
But Ekeus said Iraq's Deputy Prime Minister Tareq Aziz had pledged to address the matter "and I am happy to say we got a very understanding response from the Iraqi side".
He said that at times the safety of pilots and experts working for the U.N. Special Commission (UNSCOM), which he heads, were at risk. He gave no further details.
"This is a concern which we will obviously report to the (U.N.) Security Council," he told a news conference. His six-monthly report on Iraq is due at the council on April 11.

The U.N. official arrived in Baghdad on Thursday to try again to resolve remaining disarmament issues holding up the lifting of the international oil embargo on Iraq, imposed for its 1990 invasion of Kuwait.
He said three days of talks had failed to clear up key issues.

"We did not solve any substantive issues. There I must say there is a slight disappointment...But what we did achieve was agreement on how to proceed for the nearest future," Ekeus said in Baghdad before leaving for Bahrain.
He said he still had serious concerns over Iraq's biological warfare programme. During the talks, Iraqi officials had promised to do their best to address his concerns.

In the chemical warfare sphere, Ekeus said he had told Iraq that he still needed to resolve "seven important issues...If we manage to settle them we will come close to...ending the chemical file programme."
He said international experts were analysing the engines of Iraqi long-range missiles which his commission removed from Baghdad for analysis in the United States.

Iraq scrapped and buried the engines without U.N. supervision in 1992. UNSCOM is having them tested to determine whether any forbidden missiles -- those with a range greater than 150 km (93 miles) -- remain unaccounted for.
Ekeus declined comment on reports that he was expected to leave his post by the end of the year to become Sweden's ambassador in Washington.
